item.title: Fri Night · Selected Shorts: A First Time for Everything
item.itunes:title: Fri Night · Selected Shorts: A First Time for Everything
item.description:
On this week’s SELECTED SHORTS, Meg Wolitzer presents three stories about “firsts.” In “I Don’t Know What You’re Talking About,” by Cyn Vargas, three generations of women navigate “the talk”. The reader is Florencia Cuenca. A young man learns that you can say a lot by saying nothing at all in Elizabeth McCracken’s “A Splinter,” read by Andy Mientus. And in Jessica Treadway’s “First Day,” a woman views getting sacked as a new beginning. It’s read by Carrie Coon.

From Selected Shorts, first released November 19, 2026.

item.title: Thu PM · The Book Club | PragerU: Mike Benz: Moby-Dick by Herman Melville | The Book Club | PragerU
item.itunes:title: Thu PM · The Book Club | PragerU: Mike Benz: Moby-Dick by Herman Melville | The Book Club | PragerU
item.description:
This episode of The Book Club features Michael Knowles joined by Mike Benz, executive director of the Foundation for Freedom Online, to discuss Herman Melville’s Moby-Dick. Together, they explore Ishmael’s restless voyage to sea, the novel’s many biblical allusions, and the question at its center. Is Captain Ahab a madman consumed by revenge or a great man of history with an indomitable will? Knowles sees in Ahab the dark side of individualism. Benz makes a contrarian case for the captain who would risk everything to face the whale.

Moby-Dick offers a timeless challenge for young men who may feel adrift in today’s culture: Find a mission bigger than yourself, and choose carefully what kind of man you become along the way.

item.title: Thu AM · Planet Money: The Chicken Tax (Classic)
item.itunes:title: Thu AM · Planet Money: The Chicken Tax (Classic)
item.description:
Note: This episode originally ran in 2015 .

German families in the 60s loved tasty, cheap American-raised chicken that was suddenly coming in after the war. And Americans were loving fun, cheap Volkswagen Beetles. This arrangement was too good to last.

Today on the show, how a trade dispute over frozen chicken parts changed the American auto industry as we know it.

This episode was reported by Robert Smith and Sonari Glinton. It was produced by Frances Harlow.

item.title: Wed PM · Philosophize This!: Episode #004 ... Plato
item.itunes:title: Wed PM · Philosophize This!: Episode #004 ... Plato
item.description:
In this week's episode, we learn about Plato's "Symposium", which you might think of as philosophy's version of fan fiction. We also learn about Plato's "Theory of Forms" and ask ourselves what makes a tree, well, a tree. This leads to discussion of Plato's famous "Allegory of the Cave" and calls into question whether or not everything we see is merely a shadow of its true self. Finally, we learn about Plato's views on society and government and why he thought democracy was one of the worst forms of government, second only to tyranny. item.description:
Your money might be fueling the AI boom … just as some AI data center bets are starting to look riskier. If you own stocks, that money is likely tied up in giant tech companies like Microsoft and Nvidia. item.title: Tue AM · Planet Money: How bodegas led to the Yemeni coffeehouse explosion
item.itunes:title: Tue AM · Planet Money: How bodegas led to the Yemeni coffeehouse explosion
item.description:
There is a long-standing tradition of different immigrant groups arriving in the U.S. and specializing in one particular type of business. Think, nail salons run by people from Vietnam or Gujarati Indians owning motels and hotels.

Yemenis are another immigrant community that has largely clustered around one industry, in their case, bodegas and small grocery stores. There are thousands of these shops all over the country, despite Yemeni-Americans only making up around one-fortieth of one percent of the U.S. population, according to the last census. 

In the past 9 years, a new business success story has been built on top of that foundation: Yemeni coffee houses.

Today on the show, why some immigrant groups concentrate in a single industry, while others spread out to work in all sorts of jobs. And what it’s like for the next generation to try to expand on their parents’ success.
